claims.text: The GI application describes Machilipatnam Kalamkari as visually identified by all-over floral twine and Persian designs, block printed by traditional laborious methods with natural vegetable dyes.

quotes.quote: "Machilipatnam Kalamkari " visually identified by the all over floral twine / Persian designs which are block printed and produced in traditional laborious methods using natural vegetable dyes

claims.text: The Machilipatnam or Pedana style is one of the two main kalamkari styles of India, the other being the Srikalahasti style.

quotes.quote: The Machilipatnam style of Kalamkari or Pedana style of Kalamkari is one of the two styles of Kalamkari works present in India, with the other being, Srikalahasti style.
There are two main types of kalamkari practised from the olden days - Srikalahasti and Machilipatnam
While Pedana and Machilipatnam are the hub for hand block-printed Kalamkari, Srikalahasti in Chittoor district of Andhra Pradesh is known for the pen-drawn format.

claims.text: Machilipatnam designs are first block printed with carved wooden blocks and then coloured, whereas Srikalahasti textiles are painted entirely with pens.

quotes.quote: While in Srikalahasti, the textiles are literally painted with pens made out of bamboo and cotton, in Machilipatnam, the line drawing done with a pen is transferred onto wooden blocks which are carved and then used to print fabric.
the designs on the Masulipatnam specimens are firstly block printed and then the colours are painted with a kalam, whereas in the case of the Kalahasti product the entire work is Kalamkari

claims.text: The Krishna district administration says production is geographically limited to Pedana town and its neighbouring villages of Machilipatnam, Polavaram and Kappaladoddi in Guduru mandal of Krishna district.

quotes.quote: Production of Machilipatnam Kalamkari is geographically limited to Pedana town and its neighboring Villages of Machilipatnam, Polavaram and Kappaladoddi in Guduru mandal of Krishna district.

claims.text: The GI application says that apart from Machilipatnam and Pedana, the major production centres, parts of Polavaram and Kappaldoddi villages in Gudur mandal of Krishna District and Chirala of Prakasham District also produce Machilipatnam Kalamkari.

quotes.quote: Apart from M achilipatnam and Pedana the major pr oduction centers of Kalamkari, parts of Polavaram and Kappaldoddi villages of Gudur Mandal of Krishna District and

claims.text: Pedana is a small town just 13 km from Machilipatnam, the headquarters of Krishna district in coastal Andhra Pradesh.

quotes.quote: Pedana is a small town just 13 km from Machilipatnam, the head quarter of Krishna district in coastal Andhra Pradesh.

claims.text: The GI application places Pedana on the Machilipatnam-Vijayawada broad-gauge railway line at a distance of 10 kilometres from Machilipatnam.

quotes.quote: Pedana town is situated in M achlipatnam-Gudivada highway road and it is also situated on the Machlipatnam -Vijayawada broad-gauge railway line at a distance of 10kms from Machlipatnam

claims.text: Pedana, a small town near Machilipatnam, is the largest hub in the country for hand-block-printed kalamkari, press reports say.

quotes.quote: Pedana, a small town near the coastal town of Machilipatnam is the largest hub in the country for hand block printed Kalamkari.
Pedana is the famous home of the handmade block-printed kalamkari fabric, and almost the entire supply of it across the country comes from here.

claims.text: There is evidence of extensive trade in the dyed sheets of Masulipatnam as early as the close of the first century of the present era.

quotes.quote: There is evidence of the extensive trade in the dyed sheets of Masulipatnam as early as the close of the first century of the present era.

claims.text: It is believed that Masulipatnam's hand-printed cloth was popular with the ancient Greeks before Christ, and the Greeks under Alexander are said to have acquired it.

quotes.quote: It is believed that the hand printed cloth of Masulipatnam was popular with the ancient Greeks even before Christ.

It is believed that the indus try existed in this part of India even in the pre-Christian era. It is said that in the ancient days the Buddhist Chaitya Viharas were decorated with Kalamkari cloth and even the Greeks under Alexander are said to have acquired this cloth.

claims.text: The Imperial Gazetteer of India of 1908 records that Masulipatnam turned out admirable hand-printed chintzes for many centuries, sometimes hard to distinguish from the finest embroidery.

quotes.quote: In Masulipatnam and elsewhere in Southern India, admirable chintzes have for many centuries been turned out, which are really hand printed textiles, so perfectly coloured that it is some times difficult to distinguish them from the finest emb roidery.

claims.text: Calico printing and dyeing at Masulipatnam held sway till about the mid-18th century; the Industrial Revolution and the 1721 ban on calicos into England dealt it a death-blow.

quotes.quote: Thus the calico printing and dyeing industry of Masulipatnam held an undaunted sway till about the middle of the 18th century. The Industrial Revolution of th~ West and the banning of calicos into England in 1721 gave a death-blow to this industry.

claims.text: By the middle of the twentieth century it had become almost impossible to find anyone practising the craft in Masulipatnam.

quotes.quote: By the middle of the present century it became almost im possible to locate anyone who practised this craft in Masulipatnam.

claims.text: Most of the households of the Kapu community practised the kalamkari industry in Masulipatnam.

quotes.quote: Most of the households of Kapu com munity practised the Kalamkari Industry.

claims.text: Telagas, who formed the lower middle class of Masulipatnam town and lived there in good numbers, had taken up the kalamkari industry.

quotes.quote: Telagas who form the lower middle class inhabited Masulipatnam town in good numbers and they had taken up to thi') industry

claims.text: Under the Golconda rulers the industry received a further fillip through contact with the Persians, Masulipatnam being an important sea port of the Golconda kingdom.

quotes.quote: Undtr the Golconda rulers the industry received a further fillip with the contact of the Persians. Masulipatnam was an important commercial sea port of the Golconda Kingdom.

claims.text: The rulers of Golconda patronised the kalamkari of Masulipatnam during the 16th and 17th centuries, when textiles were made for the Sultanate and for Persia.

quotes.quote: The rulers at Golconda patronised Kalamkari of Masulipatnam (Now called Machilipatnam), during the 16th and 17th centuries. The textiles were made for the Sultanate of Golconda and Persia/Iran.

claims.text: The GI application relates that some enterprising Persian merchants settled in Masulipatnam with their families, introduced new designs and, with local skilled workmen, produced large quantities for export.

quotes.quote: Some enterprising Persian merchants settled down in M asulipatnam with their families intr oduced new designs and with the help of local skilled workmen, produced large quantities for export.

claims.text: Persia stopped importing Masulipatnam kalamkari in 1930, and after about 1930 the industry had a great downfall and became almost forgotten.

quotes.quote: the stoppage of imports of these products into Persia in the year 1930 badly affec ted the industry.
But, after about 1930, the industry had a great downfall and very soon it had become almost a forgotten industry.

claims.text: Masulipatnam kalamkari had been exported to Persia since the 17th century, but in 1924 the link with Persia was broken.

quotes.quote: Kalamkari from Masulipatnam was being exported to Persia since 17th century onwards and Kalahasti was an important centre after the second half of the 19th century. however in 1924, the link with Persia/Iran was broken.

claims.text: It is understood that kalamkari products won medals at the London Wembley Exhibition of 1924, medals their awardee Venkataswamy Naidu preserved.

quotes.quote: At the London Wembly Exhibition in 1924 it is understood that the excellence of Kalamkari products was recognised by the award of medals.
Plate 19 shows the medals proudly preserved by their awardee Shri Venkataswamy Naidu himself.

claims.text: In 1952 the kalamkari workers tried to sell their goods through a few Madras firms, but the industry still languished.

quotes.quote: In 1952 the Kalamkari workers tried to sell their goods through a few Madras firms. The industry still languished.

claims.text: In 1952 kalamkari was revived at Masulipatnam with the help of the All India Handicrafts Board under Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay.

quotes.quote: the All India Handicrafts Board under Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay revived the craft in 1952.
In 1952 Kalamkari was revived at Masulipatnam at the instigation of some local textile lovers and with the help of the All India Handicrafts board

quotes.quote: He first started it in early 1970s in Polavaram with his partners. But the partnership fell through very soon and he came back to his hometown Pedana and started the first Kalamkari firm in 1972, that made and sold hand block-printed Kalamkari commercially.

claims.text: Textile designer Nelly H. Sethna transformed the static designs of Machilipatnam in the 1970s, bringing out old block designs and rearranging motifs into new patterns.

quotes.quote: Nelly H. Sethana, textile designer transformed the static designs of Machilipatnam in the 1970s. She brought out old block designs and rearranged many motifs to create new patterns.
Nelly H. Sethna revitalised the designs in th 1970s.

claims.text: Sethna also stopped the bleaching of the cloth in the final stage, leaving an off-white background with a pleasing, warm effect.

quotes.quote: She also stopped the bleaching of the cloth in the final stage leading to an off-white background which lent a pleasing and warm effect overall.

claims.text: Asia InCH writes that hand block printing evolved from the dye-painted fabrics of the Coromandel Coast called Machilipatnam paintings, renowned trade items of the seventeenth century, mainly to European countries and Iran.

quotes.quote: Hand block printing evolves from the dye painted fabrics of Coromandel Coast referred to as Machilipatnam paintings.
These paintings were renowned trade items of seventeenth century mainly to European countries and Iran.

claims.text: As a trade textile it was called chintz by the English, sitz by the Dutch and pintado by the Portuguese.

quotes.quote: As a trade textile it was known by several names: chintz by the English, sitz by the Dutch and pintado by the Portuguese.
The English called it chintz, the Dutch called it sitz, the Portugese pintado.

claims.text: Kalams were replaced by blocks in the nineteenth century, block printing taking over from pen-drawn chintz as the designs were repetitive.

quotes.quote: Eventually the kalam's were replaced by blocks in the nineteenth century.
Originally chintz textiles were Indian cotton cloth with a pattern applied with a bamboo pen or kalam and by dyeing with mordants and resists. Later, block printing took over.
Slowly the shift from 'kalam' to the block happened as the designs were repetitive.

claims.text: A Machilipatnam cotton dated 1879, probably made for export to Iran, carries a Persian inscription calling it qalamkar, a printed imitation of hand-drawn kalamkari.

quotes.quote: This cotton was probably made for export to Iran. A printed inscription in Persian names the trader (Sayyid Muhammad Mahdi), gives the date and labels the piece a'la numuneh ('superior example').
It also calls the textile Qalamkar, as it is a printed imitation of the region's traditional hand-drawn kalamkari decoration.
Textile, animal design, kalamkari (pen work) and block printing on cotton, Machilipatnam, dated AH 1297/1879 AD

claims.text: A Machilipatnam prayer mat of 1908 was hand-printed in black, red, yellow and blue from well-worn wood-blocks of an earlier period.

quotes.quote: Mohammedan prayer mat (Janamaz) in hand-printed calico, Machilipatnam, 1908.
Mohammedan prayer mat (Janamaz) in hand-printed calico in four colours black, red, yellow and blue. Taken from well-worn wood-blocks of an earlier period.

claims.text: In step a of the GI method, grey cloth bought from textile mills in batches of 100 metres or more is cut into 10 to 15 metre pieces.

quotes.quote: 3.2 Process of Kalamkari Block Printing: a) Grey Cloth Cutting: Batches of 100 meters or above are purchased from textile mills in bulk.
The grey cloth purchased is then cut into pieces of length varying from 10 -15 meters as per the working unit capacity and customer demand/ end use.

claims.text: In step b, kora cloth is bleached white without bleaching powder by soaking overnight in buffalo or goat dung solution and washing in flowing water, over four or five days.

quotes.quote: b) Bleaching Cora Cloth: bleaching process is carried out using buffalo dung solution without using bleaching powder and facilitated by sunshine. It takes 4-5 days for getting the cloth white.
The kora long cloth which is cut to the required sizes is soaked in a goat or buffalo dung solution in a big pot.
The cloth is kept soaked throughout the night and the next morning it is
cleaned in the flowing water of a river or canal and then dried on the water weeds. This bleaching process is repeated for four or five days

claims.text: No chemical bleaching powder is used, as it is believed to weaken the cloth and to have a deleterious effect on the dyes.

quotes.quote: No chemical bleaching powder should be uscd in this process. It is believed that the usage of bleaching powder will adversely affect the strength of the cloth as also will have a deleterious effect on the dyes applied

claims.text: The Krishna district account scours grey cloth by boiling it 2-3 hours in a hot alkaline solution such as soda ash, caustic soda or detergent, making the fibre more absorbent.

quotes.locator: Process involved in Block printing, scouring
quotes.quote: In order to make fibre more absorbent to obtain more even shades, penetration of the dye stuff the natural impurities have to be removed by boiling the cloth in hot alkaline solution like soda ash and caustic soda or detergent for 2-3 hrs at boiling temperature.

claims.text: In step c, the white cloth is soaked evenly in myrobalan juice and dried in sunlight, the myrobalan acting as a mordant for block printing.

quotes.quote: c) Application of Myrobalam: the white cloth is soaked in myrobalam juice in suach a way that it is equally distributed all over the cloth. It is then dried in sunlight. Myrobalam acts as a mordant for block printing.

claims.text: It is said that treating the cloth with myrobalan and buffalo milk prevents the dyes from spreading or smudging when they are applied.

quotes.quote: It is said that the milk prevents the spreading of the dye on application.
The next step involves treating the cloth with Myrobalan seeds and buffalo milk to prevent smudging of dyes when painted.

claims.text: Karakkaya, the dried unripe fruit of myrobalan or Terminalia chebula, is listed as a mordant among the plant sources used in Kalamkari production.

lede.text: The GI application describes Machilipatnam Kalamkari as visually identified by all-over floral twine and Persian designs, block printed by traditional laborious methods with natural vegetable dyes.
Production is centred on Pedana town and nearby Machilipatnam, Polavaram and Kappaladoddi in Krishna district, Andhra Pradesh; the GI application adds Chirala.
It is one of the two main kalamkari styles: Machilipatnam designs are first block printed with carved wooden blocks, whereas Srikalahasti textiles are painted with pens.
Production is carried out in karkhanas, commercial workshops where block makers, washers and printers work under the same roof.

sentences.text: There is evidence of extensive trade in the dyed sheets of Masulipatnam as early as the close of the first century of the present era.
The rulers of Golconda patronised the kalamkari of Masulipatnam during the 16th and 17th centuries, and contact with the Persians gave the industry a further fillip.
The GI application relates that some enterprising Persian merchants settled in Masulipatnam and, with the help of local skilled workmen, produced large quantities for export.
Calico printing and dyeing at Masulipatnam held sway till about the mid-18th century; the Industrial Revolution and the 1721 ban on calicos into England dealt it a death-blow.
A V&A cover of the 1800s was catalogued as printed in Masulipatam by Iranian craftsmen for the Iranian market, and sources differ on when the Persian trade ended, giving 1924 and 1930.
By the middle of the twentieth century it had become almost impossible to find anyone practising the craft in Masulipatnam.
Sources also differ on 1952: in one account the industry still languished, while others say kalamkari was revived at Masulipatnam with the help of the All India Handicrafts Board.

The GI application says that around 1968 many families of the professional weavers' community moved into kalamkari, and The News Minute reports that Pitchuka Veera Subbaiah started Pedana's first kalamkari firm in 1972.
In the GI method, grey cloth from textile mills is cut into 10 to 15 metre pieces and bleached white in dung solution over four or five days, without bleaching powder.
The white cloth is soaked in myrobalan juice, which acts as a mordant for block printing, and dried in sunlight.
Designs are then printed by hand with wooden blocks for outline, background and filling; for polychromatic designs the black and red portions are printed first.

After the printed cloth has been kept 2-3 days for the colours to dry, it is washed in flowing water to remove the excess gum and then boiled for two hours, with madder added for red and pomegranate rind for yellow.

The cloth is starched with boiled rice water and milk, secondary colours such as yellow, pink, green and blue are printed and a few dyed portions resisted with wax, and alum water makes all the colours fast.
Washing with soap is the last and final process, after which the cloth is dried in the sun, folded and pressed for sale.

In the method the Census monograph describes, beeswax applied with a hair-padded kalam covers all areas except those to be dyed blue, the cloth is dipped in the indigo vat, and the wax is removed by boiling.

Sources differ on wax even within the GI application: its method resists a few dyed portions with wax, while it names a few master craftsmen who then practised a revised block printing method using no wax process and no painting.
In the Census of India 1961 account, the base was mill-made kora, unbleached long cloth of 40 or 60 counts.
Kasim black is made by fermenting rust-free iron pieces with jaggery and water in closed earthen pots for three weeks and adding gum arabic, though MAP Academy says the black comes from iron ore.
Karam, the red printing mordant, is babul gum solution mixed with an alum decoction, while MAP Academy says the red is made from alum and tamarind seed powder.
From about 1918 alizarin imported from Germany, called peepa colour, came into common use, and manjista or madder was used with it once chiranji bark was no longer available.
Yellow is made by boiling 100 grams of myrobalan flowers in a litre of water and adding about 10 grams of alum powder.
The indigo vat takes crushed tandipa ginjalu seeds, which the GI application calls Atta or Annetto seeds and the Census monograph cassia allata, with indigo cakes and lime.
Plant sources include karakkaya, the dried unripe myrobalan fruit, as a mordant, moduga flowers as a dye, and jajaku leaves as a dyeing auxiliary.
Blocks are carved from teak, preferred for its fine grain and strength, though a 2019 account says they are now made from lighter wood; finished blocks are soaked in groundnut oil for 5-6 days.
Kasam gives a permanent black on cloth soaked in myrobalan, a tannin-based mordant, but not on plain cloth.

The GI application says alum improves the brightness and fastness of red and pink and myrobalan the fixation of dye, especially black, and that all the colours, temporary until then, become fast in alum water.
Sources differ on the red: the GI method prints a karam of gum and alum, while Rajarshi Sengupta writes that alum solution is not used at Machilipatnam for the red colour.
In chintz making, areas with an alum mordant become red and those with an iron mordant black, while indigo needs no mordant and the areas not to become blue are resisted, usually with wax.
The GI method lists caustic soda and hydrosulphate among the raw materials for the indigo blue.

Chintz techniques are associated with the Coromandel Coast because of a favourable combination of chemicals in its soil, water and dye plants, and the GI application lists a peculiar richness in Machilipatnam's water.
Masulipatnam designs evolved to meet three demands: export to Persia and the Middle East, export to Western countries, and domestic and Far-Eastern markets.
Bed sheets, curtains and prayer cloths for the Middle East carried typical Persian designs, while products for Western countries generally carried floral and animal designs.
Machilipatnam kalamkari usually carries Persian motifs such as creepers, lotus and twines, and its motifs often combine local forms with ones derived from Persia and Europe.

The GI application names forms of the lotus flower, the cartwheel, parrots and an interlacing pattern of leaves and flowers as leitmotifs, and lists stylised flora and fauna with zig-zag outlines and pointed edges among its distinctive features.
The main colours are black, red, blue, yellow and green, with chocolate made by mixing red and black in the ratio 3:1 and pink by adding water to the red.
In the 1970s Nelly H. Sethna rearranged old block motifs into new patterns and stopped the final bleaching of the cloth, leaving an off-white background.
Popular border designs include muthyala pandiri, a pandal studded with gems, and gandabherunda, the double bird.
Geographical indication application 90 was filed on 16 April 2007 by the Vegetable Hand-block Kalamkari Printers Association of Pedana mandal, Krishna district.
Other accounts state that Pedana kalamkari was included in the Geographical Indications Registry in 2012, or received a geographical indications tag in 2013.
In the Census of India 1961 survey at Masulipatnam, 11 families of Telagas and ex-tappers did dyeing and printing, and a block printer was paid Rs. 3.50 a day.
In August 2004 kalamkari sold in retail outlets in Andhra Pradesh at Rs. 100 to 200 per metre.
By 2019 a large majority of Pedana's kalamkari was screen-printed with chemical colours, as villagers took up screen printing with large stencils to meet demand and cut costs.

The News Minute reported that washing screen-printed kalamkari in ponds was polluting the water, and that in the past the Krishna District Collector had sent out a few notices to those using chemical colours, warning them of action.
A 2023 craft survey of the Machilipatnam Kalamkari cluster found production waste, including plant-based mordants and dyes, disposed of in garbage bins or local canals.
According to Varun Pitchuka, the water of the Krishna River has the correct mineral composition to help the colours develop and set.
Pedana is a small town near Machilipatnam, the headquarters of Krishna district: 13 km away in one account and 10 kilometres in the GI application.

The GI application states that Chirala of Prakasham District also produces Machilipatnam Kalamkari products, and the Bapatla district administration lists Chirala among Bapatla District's revenue divisions.
The industry apparently developed around Masulipatnam because dye materials were at hand, clean Krishna river water flowed in a nearby canal, and saline soils were available.
Rajarshi Sengupta writes that in Machilipatnam the cotton fabrics are washed at the Kalia Canal, and that a canal emptying into the Bay of Bengal is the source of water there.
In the Census of India 1961 account, the blue dye came from the indigo plant, then grown quite commonly in Krishna District.
